correctness.rationale: Every connected bipartite graph on each n=7,8,9 has shores a<=b and arises from one of the explicitly enumerated 0<=mask<2^(ab) incidence matrices; disconnected graphs are excluded. BFS path counts satisfy an induction on distance. An independent Floyd--Warshall plus distance-DAG path-count implementation agrees on each exhaustive fixed-shore maximum and count, and independently reports every extremal missing-degree profile. A third BFS program agrees on all order-nine profile counts. Missing-degree profiles mathematically force the stated isomorphism types. For the exceptional graph, independent pairwise shortest-path calculation gives 9+16+20+36+24=105 and diameter four. This proves finite statements only; no infinite inference.

originality.rationale: The arXiv:2604.04907v1 primary full text (including the statement of Problem 15) asks for all bipartite maximizers. Its stated results are general bounds and restricted graph families, not the global small-order classification. The public diameter-two theorem covers only diameter-two graphs and cannot imply three- and four-diameter extremizers; the other close full-text record concerns path blow-ups and large-order constructions. The finite claim resolves all extremizers at orders seven through nine, including a diameter-four equality graph not belonging to the matching-deletion subfamily. Scientific literature and semantic searches found no stronger covering result. Equivalent unindexed work remains a genuine residual risk.
residual_risks: An equivalent small-order classification could appear in an unindexed, unpublished or inaccessible work.
The proof is computationally exhaustive for finite orders and has not been externally audited.

value.rationale: The motivating 2026 primary literature explicitly asks for fixed-order bipartite gpn maximizers. This gives the first full three previously-unresolved order layers n=7,8,9, including all equality graphs and exact counts, rather than computing a narrow arbitrary slice. The additional diameter-four coextremizer at n=9 is structurally unexpected and shows that restricting searches to matching deletions would omit true global maximizers. The result is a motivated finite cutoff with a complete certificate, not an unsupported asymptotic claim.
